segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous one,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And by this we know that we have come to know him: if we keep his commandments.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who says,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I have come to know him,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in that person;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but whoever keeps his word, in that person the love of God has truly been made complete. By this we know that we are in him:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the one who says he remains in him ought himself to walk just as he walked.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, I am not writing you a new commandment, but an old commandment that you have had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you heard.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the other hand, I am writing you a new commandment, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who says he is in the light and hates his brother is in the darkness even now.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who loves his brother remains in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but the one who hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven on account of his name.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am writing to you, fathers, because you have come to know the one who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have written to you, children, because you have come to know the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you have come to know the one who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have overcome the evil one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because everything in the world, the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and the boastful pride in possessions, is not from the Father but is from the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the world is passing away, and its desire with it, but the one who does the will of God remains forever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Children, it is the last hour, and just as you heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. From this we know that it is the last hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us. But they went out so that it might be revealed that none of them is of us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you all know.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have not written to you because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is from the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who is the liar, if not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist: the one who denies the Father and the Son.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either; the one who acknowledges the Son has the Father also.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As for you, let what you heard from the beginning remain in you. If what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this is the promise that he himself promised us: eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have written these things to you about those who are trying to lead you astray.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As for you, the anointing that you received from him remains in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about all things, and is true and is no lie, and just as it has taught you, remain in him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he is revealed we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If you know that he is righteous, you know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.

notes.note: The word was used of someone who speaks up on another's behalf, as a supporter might before a judge. In John's Gospel the same word is used of the Spirit, where older English versions have 'Comforter'. Here it is Jesus who speaks for believers before the Father, and English versions have long used 'advocate' in this verse.

The word belongs to the Septuagint's vocabulary of atonement and the forgiveness it brings. 'Propitiation' (turning away wrath) and 'expiation' (removing sin) each take one side of a long-running dispute. 'Atoning sacrifice', used by several modern versions, leaves that question open. The noun occurs in the New Testament only here and at 4:10.

The Greek can mean a person's love for God, God's love for that person, or the kind of love that comes from God. The translation keeps the open phrase. The same question arises with 'the love of the Father' in verse 15, where love for the Father is the more likely sense because it is set against loving the world.

The traditional 'abide' has dropped out of ordinary English. The Greek verb is the everyday word for staying or remaining, and the letter uses it repeatedly, of people remaining in God, of God's word remaining in them, and in verse 19 of those who did not remain with the community. One English verb is used throughout so that the repetition can be heard.
The Greek here switches to a distinct pronoun, literally 'that one', which in this letter regularly points to Jesus. 'Walk' is the common Jewish idiom for how a person conducts their life.

In this letter 'brother' means a fellow member of the believing community, whether a man or a woman, not a sibling. Some modern versions render 'brother or sister' or 'fellow believer'. The masculine singular here and in the following verses is generic.

notes.phrase: in him there is no cause for stumbling
notes.traditional: there is none occasion of stumbling in him
notes.note: The word refers to a trap or obstacle that makes someone fall. The Greek may mean that there is nothing in such a person to trip him up, or nothing in him that makes others fall. The pronoun could also be read as 'in it', meaning that in the light there is nothing to stumble over.

Throughout verses 12 to 14 the Greek conjunction can mean either 'because' (giving the reason for writing) or 'that' (giving the content of what is written, as in 'I write to tell you that your sins have been forgiven'). Most translations choose 'because', but the other reading is well supported.

The verb shifts from the present tense in verses 12 and 13 to a past tense here. Most interpreters take this as a stylistic variation that still refers to the present letter, since Greek letter-writers often used a past tense from the reader's point of view. Some think an earlier writing is meant. Some editions and translations number the first sentence of this verse as the end of verse 13.

The first noun means showy boasting or pretension. The word for 'life' here is not the one used for eternal life but the one for livelihood or material means, as at 3:17. The traditional 'pride of life' suggests pride in being alive or in life generally, whereas the Greek points to showing off what one has. Several modern versions render it similarly ('pride in riches', 'pride in one's possessions').

The word occurs in the New Testament only in 1 and 2 John. Its prefix can mean both 'against' and 'in place of', so it names an opponent of Christ or a rival claimant to his place. The author assumes that his readers already expect such a figure and applies the term to those who have left the community and deny that Jesus is the Christ (verses 19 and 22).

The Greek word is closely related to 'Christ' (the anointed one) and so also to 'antichrist': the readers have an anointing where the opponents are anti-anointed. Most interpreters take the anointing to be the Holy Spirit given to believers. Some take it as the teaching they received at the beginning, or both together.

Many later manuscripts read 'you know all things', which the King James Version follows. The reading translated here, 'you all know', is found in important early manuscripts and is preferred by most modern editors. It fits the argument that knowledge belongs to every member of the community and not to a select few.

The Greek verb form can be either a command ('remain') or a statement ('you remain'), and the pronoun can mean 'in him' or 'in it', that is, in the anointing or its teaching. The command reading is chosen because the next verse repeats the same words as an unmistakable command. The long sentence leading up to it can also be punctuated in more than one way.

The word means arrival and the presence that follows. It was the regular term for the state visit of a king or high official, an occasion for which a city prepared itself. This is its only occurrence in the letters and Gospel of John.

Used across the New Testament for fellow believers of either sex, and translations split between 'brother', 'brother or sister' and 'fellow believer'; it needs one policy for singular and plural.
Recurs in the Gospels and Paul with renderings ranging from 'stumbling block' and 'offence' to 'trap'; it should be consistent, together with the verb σκανδαλίζω.
